background: Male, junior, studying for grad school entrance exams. Second session, talking about how studying is going.
context:
Counsellor: How has this week been?
Client: Same as always, I guess. Kind of flat.
utterance: I've basically been in the library until it closes every single day this semester. And I still get back to my room feeling like I got nothing done. My roommates are all doing internships. It's just me in there running problem sets.
surface: In the library until closing every day; still feels nothing got accomplished back in his room; roommates are all interning while he alone studies for the exam.
emotions: Frustration; loneliness.
meaning: He doubts whether all this effort will actually buy him anything; he has taken a different road from his peers and no one is walking it with him.

background: Female, sophomore, came in over conflict with her roommates. First session.
context:
Counsellor: Where would you like to start?
Client: Just... the roommate thing, I guess.
utterance: Last week they rearranged the beds. The three of them worked it out first and then told me, and they gave the spot by the window to the new transfer girl. I didn't say anything, I just moved. Then this week they made plans to go out and didn't ask me.
surface: The other three settled the bed rearrangement before telling her; the window spot went to the new transfer student; she said nothing and moved; she was not invited to this week's outing.
emotions: The hurt of being left out; a sense of being wronged.
meaning: She feels she barely registers in that room; going along quietly is her way of not making things worse, but the cost is that nobody knows how she feels.

background: Male, second-year master's student, tense relationship with his father. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: Last time you said you wanted to talk about family.
Client: Yeah. I went home this past weekend.
utterance: At dinner my dad asked what I'm doing after I graduate. I said I want to work for a couple of years and then see. He put his chopsticks down and said all these years of school and that's all I amount to. Nobody talked for the rest of the meal. I moved my train ticket up and went back to campus.
surface: His father asked about post-graduation plans; he said he wants to work a couple of years first; his father put down his chopsticks and said all that schooling amounted to nothing; the table went silent; he left for campus early.
emotions: Hurt; anger with nowhere to go.
meaning: A plan he had thought seriously about was dismissed in one line; leaving early was the only protest available to him.

background: Female, first-year, struggling to adjust. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: How was this week?
Client: Same, I guess... busy.
utterance: I joined three clubs, so there's something every evening and meetings on weekends. My mom called to ask how I'm doing and I told her great, really full schedule. Then I hung up and sat on my bed and suddenly had no idea what I'm even busy with.
surface: Joined three clubs with activities every evening and weekend meetings; told her mother she is doing great and keeping full; after hanging up had no idea what she is busy with.
emotions: Emptiness; disorientation.
meaning: She fills the calendar to avoid how hard adjusting has been; she gives her mother only the good news, so the real confusion has nowhere to go.
affect: bright tone that slows down at the end

background: Male, senior, internship going badly. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You wrote "the internship" on your intake form.
Client: Yeah, that's the thing lately.
utterance: My supervisor had me put together a data report. I pulled two all-nighters on it. She glanced at it, said the formatting was wrong, told me to redo it. So I redid it. She's never mentioned it since. I don't even know if she used it.
surface: Two all-nighters to finish the report; the supervisor glanced at it, called the formatting wrong and ordered a redo; after the redo she never brought it up or said whether it was used.
emotions: Deflation; the specific frustration of going unseen.
meaning: The redo is not what stings — it is that the effort drew no response at all; the open question of whether it was ever used leaves him unsure his work meant anything.

background: Male, first-year. Money got tight at home (he has not gone into detail). Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Last time you mentioned you'd started working.
Client: Yeah, picked up a few things.
utterance: It's nothing, really, just busy. I'm in the dining hall at six in the morning, then back for two hours at lunch, and some nights I hand out flyers. Classes are fine. Eight a.m. ones are rough, I got marked absent twice last week.
surface: Dining hall at 6 a.m., two more hours at lunch, flyers some evenings — three jobs in a day; can't make 8 a.m. classes; marked absent twice last week.
emotions: Exhaustion; the awkwardness of not wanting to look like he's struggling.
meaning: He compresses the whole weight of it into "it's nothing"; the absences are the sign that he can't keep this up, but he does not want it treated as a problem.
affect: offhand, like it happened to someone else

background: Female, first-year master's student, half a year in. Second session, talking about research progress.
context:
Counsellor: You said last time you wanted to talk about your project.
Client: It's nothing big, just catching up on how things are.
utterance: Things are okay. Lab stuff is scattered — I order reagents, I make the cleaning rota, and a senior student is rushing her defence so I ran data for her for two weeks. My own project is... still at the reading stage. My advisor asked about progress last week and I said almost there.
surface: Handles reagent orders, cleaning rota and other chores; ran data for a senior student for two weeks; her own project is stalled at the literature stage; told her advisor she is "almost there".
emotions: Anxiety; a resentment she cannot voice.
meaning: Her time goes to everyone else's work while her own project sits still — "things are okay" and "almost there" are the same act of keeping up appearances; the real stall has been said to no one.
affect: easy tone, but the details keep piling up

background: Female, first-year master's student, seeking help over her relationship with her advisor. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: You mentioned you haven't wanted to go into the lab since last week's group meeting.
Client: Yeah... it started that day.
utterance: In lab meeting last week, right after my presentation, he said in front of everyone that I've been on this topic for six months and still haven't gotten anywhere. My face went white. I was so humiliated. The last few days I've been taking the long way around the hallway to avoid him.
surface: Told in front of the whole group that six months in she still hasn't broken into the topic; went pale in the moment; has been avoiding him in the hallway since.
emotions: Humiliation; shame and fear of being dismissed again.
meaning: That sentence shook her sense of whether she belongs in this lab or in research at all; she needs someone to first acknowledge that it genuinely hurt.

background: Male, junior, struggling in a relationship. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Last time you said you hadn't been in touch since the fight.
Client: We're in touch now.
utterance: She texted back yesterday. Four words. "Busy, talk to you later." There's been no later. I stared at those four words all night. One minute I think she really is busy, the next I'm sure she just doesn't want to deal with me.
surface: Her reply was "busy, talk to you later" and nothing followed; he reread it all night; he swings between "she's genuinely busy" and "she doesn't want me".
emotions: Agitation, being kept in suspense; an unspoken fear of being left.
meaning: Those four words have left the whole relationship unresolved; he needs a definite signal, even a bad one.

background: Female, senior, came in after losing a funded graduate placement. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You wrote "the grad school thing" on the form.
Client: Yeah, results came out last week.
utterance: I missed it by a fraction of a point. That much. The day the list went up my roommate got in, and they were popping champagne in our room. I laughed along. I even took the photos for them. Then I stood out in the hallway for a long time and couldn't make myself go back in.
surface: Missed the placement by a fraction of a point; her roommate got in and celebrated in their room; she laughed along and took photos; afterwards stood in the hallway a long time, unable to go in.
emotions: Loss and bitterness held down hard; grief that had to be hidden at someone else's celebration.
meaning: She feels even her sadness is out of place — the celebration belongs to someone else, the hallway is hers; she needs somewhere she doesn't have to smile.

background: Male, third-year master's student, job-hunting pressure. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: How's the search going?
Client: I've sent out a lot...
utterance: Forty-something applications this fall. Two interviews, and both died at the second round. My parents don't know. They think I got an offer ages ago. My mom was talking me up in the family group chat last week. Every time they call I have to sit there working out how to answer.
surface: Over forty applications, only two interviews, both ending at the second round; his parents believe he already has an offer; his mother praised him in the family group chat; he has to prepare himself before every call home.
emotions: Anxiety; guilt toward his parents and the weight of keeping it from them.
meaning: He is carrying two burdens — not finding work, and not being allowed to let his parents down; the phone call has become the heaviest moment of the day.

background: Female, sophomore, low mood since her pet died. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You said the last couple of weeks have been rough.
Client: Yeah... it's a little embarrassing to say out loud.
utterance: My cat died last month. I'd had her eight years. When I brought it up with friends they said it's just a cat, get another one. So I stopped bringing it up. But I still catch myself looking down when I open my door, every single time.
surface: The cat she had for eight years died a month ago; friends said "it's just a cat, get another"; she stopped mentioning it; she still looks down out of habit when opening her door.
emotions: Deep grief; the loneliness of packing it away after not being understood.
meaning: Eight years of company was not granted the weight it deserved; not mentioning it is not letting go — it is having no one who could hold the grief.

background: Male, senior. Graduate entrance exam scores just came out. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You booked in about "the exam".
Client: Right. Scores are out.
utterance: Six points under the cutoff. I was ready for it, honestly, it's fine. The night the scores dropped I played video games with my roommate. It's just... my mom still doesn't know. She texted me that day asking and I said they weren't out yet.
surface: Scored six points below the cutoff; says he was ready for it and it's fine; played games as usual the night scores came out; told his mother the scores weren't out yet.
emotions: Loss he is bracing against; guilt and fear about facing his mother — all covered by "it's fine".
meaning: "It's fine" is anaesthetic applied in advance so it won't hurt; the lie to his mother gives away how much he actually cares.

background: Female, sophomore, parents divorced last month. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Last time you said things had changed at home.
Client: Yeah, it wasn't sudden or anything.
utterance: My parents finalised the divorce last month. Honestly it's a good thing — they fought for years, it should have happened ages ago, it's a relief for everyone. I'm fine with it, I'm an adult. It's just, I was clearing out some boxes and found a photo of the three of us from when I was little. I put it at the bottom of the box.
surface: Her parents divorced last month; she calls it a good thing, a relief, and says she is fine with it; while clearing boxes she found an old photo of the three of them and buried it at the bottom.
emotions: Grief and loss pressed flat under "it's a good thing"; longing for the family she grew up in.
meaning: Relief as an argument and loss as an experience are two different things; putting the photo at the bottom is how she handles the sadness — out of sight means not yet.
affect: brisk, with a pause at the photo

background: Female, senior, torn between a job offer and her parents' expectations. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Have you told your family about the offer?
Client: ...Not yet.
utterance: My parents have always wanted me to come home and sit the civil service exams — they say stability matters most for a girl. I got an offer from a company in Shenzhen and I still haven't been able to bring it up. They need my answer the day after tomorrow.
surface: Her parents want her home for the civil service track; she already holds a Shenzhen offer; she has not told them; she must answer in two days.
emotions: Anxiety; guilt.
meaning: This is the first decision she has made openly on her own terms; "couldn't bring it up" means she expects saying it will start a fight; what she cares about is whether her parents can see her as an adult who gets to decide.

background: Male, first-year master's student, struggling since switching fields. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: Last time you mentioned thinking about your undergrad major.
Client: Yeah, more than usual lately.
utterance: I switched into computer science back then because of the job market. I can keep up with the coursework, grades are fine. It's just, sometimes a video comes up of friends from my old music program playing a show, and I put my phone down and go stand on the balcony for a while. I wouldn't say I regret it. There's just a hollow spot.
surface: Switched to CS for employability and is doing fine academically; puts the phone down and goes to the balcony when videos of his old music classmates' shows come up; says he doesn't regret it but there's "a hollow spot".
emotions: Wistfulness; a loss he can't quite name.
meaning: What he set down was not just a major but a version of himself; the hollow spot is a shelved love reminding him it existed — he needs someone to acknowledge the choice had a cost.

background: Female, junior, long-term carer for her mother, who has depression. Fourth session.
context:
Counsellor: How were things at home this week?
Client: Same as ever with my mom.
utterance: I call her every day at lunch to remind her about her medication and listen for an hour. I turn down pretty much everything friends invite me to. One day last week I called half an hour late and she said, so you find me tiresome too. And I said no, no, of course not.
surface: Calls her mother every midday to prompt her medication and listens for an hour; turns down almost all invitations from friends; called half an hour late once and was asked "so you find me tiresome too"; she denied it immediately.
emotions: Exhaustion; an unvoiced sense of unfairness and of being trapped.
meaning: She has become her mother's only support and her own life is giving way piece by piece; behind that quick "no, of course not" is a world where even admitting tiredness feels like betrayal — she needs permission to love her mother and be worn out at once.

background: Male, senior, about to graduate and separate from close friends. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Last time you said the room felt strange lately.
Client: Not strange exactly... everyone's just doing their own thing.
utterance: There were four of us. We used to eat every meal together, play ball every day. Now one got into a program out of state, two are interning, and it's just me still on campus. I put a game in the group chat a few days ago and nobody answered for half a day. So I deleted the message.
surface: The four of them used to be inseparable; now one is away in a program, two are interning, only he remains on campus; a game invitation in the group chat went unanswered for half a day; he deleted the message.
emotions: A flat kind of loss; the embarrassment of reaching out and getting nothing.
meaning: What he deleted was not a message but the fact he doesn't want to admit — that everyone has already scattered; he is going through the goodbye early, with nobody willing to acknowledge with him that it is happening.

background: Female, second-year master's student, perfectionism and procrastination. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: How did the thesis go this week?
Client: ...Still haven't started.
utterance: I have a dozen pages of reading notes for the proposal, I've rewritten the outline four times, and I haven't written one word of the actual text. My advisor says I've prepared plenty and should just start writing. I know he's right. But every time I open the document I'm certain whatever comes out won't match what's in my head, and then I go read more papers.
surface: A dozen pages of notes and four outline revisions but no draft; her advisor says she is well prepared and should start; opening the document convinces her the writing won't match what she imagined, so she returns to reading.
emotions: Anxiety; fear of writing something bad.
meaning: Reading is safe; writing means letting an imperfect version of herself be seen; what has her stuck is not ability but the demand that "the me on the page" live up to "the me in my head" — she needs permission to write it badly first.

background: Male, senior, signed up for a year of rural teaching service; the people around him don't get it. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Last time you said your plans after graduation were settled.
Client: Yeah, signed. A year teaching out west.
utterance: My dad says I'm dodging the job market. My classmates think I'm padding a résumé, doing it for show. Whatever, let them think what they want. It's one year. I can look for work when I'm back, it's not a big deal.
surface: Signed up for a year of rural teaching service; his father calls it dodging the job market and classmates call it résumé-padding; he says "let them think what they want" and "it's not a big deal".
emotions: The hurt and isolation of not being understood, tucked behind indifference.
meaning: This is the first major choice he has made on values he actually holds, and nobody has taken it seriously; under "let them think what they want" is the wish that one person would ask him, in earnest, why he wants to go.

background: Female, junior, drew since childhood, stopped after the college entrance exams. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: Anything you'd like to get into this week?
Client: Not much... I cleared out some old stuff.
utterance: I listed my drawing tablet on a resale site. Somebody bought it the next day. I hadn't drawn in ages, it was just taking up space. Before the buyer came to pick it up I wiped it down and put a new nib on the pen.
surface: Sold her drawing tablet; says she hadn't drawn in ages and it was taking up space; before handing it over she cleaned it and fitted a new pen nib.
emotions: An unacknowledged reluctance and grief.
meaning: What she sold was not an idle object but the version of herself who drew; wiping it down and fitting a new nib was a careful goodbye she never said out loud — she needs someone to see what this "small thing" weighed.

background: Female, sophomore. Second session; last time you talked about her running for student council.
context:
Counsellor: How has the week been?
Client: Fine, I guess... the results came out.
utterance: The list went up and I wasn't on it. I spent over a month on my speech and I lost by a lot. My roommate got in, and she barely prepared.
surface: She lost the student council election; over a month of preparation, a wide margin; her roommate, who barely prepared, won.
emotions: Disappointment and embarrassment, with a sting toward the roommate (unsaid).
meaning: What hurts is less the loss than what it seems to say — that effort still wasn't enough; the comparison with her roommate makes that harder to admit.
affect: flat voice; a pause before "my roommate"
flawed: Hey, one election doesn't say anything about you. You worked really hard, and you'll get it next time.
error_note: This is reassurance: it rushes to make the disappointment go away, which tells her the feeling needn't exist. She is being moved on before she has been heard.

background: Male, first-year master's student. First session; his advisor suggested he come.
context:
Counsellor: Would you like to tell me what's been going on?
Client: Yeah... it's about my dad.
utterance: My dad called last week and said the neighbour's son is already on six figures at a tech company, and asked what grad school is even for. I said I'm working on a project, and he said "Can you eat a project?" and hung up.
surface: His father compared him with the neighbour's son's salary, questioned the point of grad school, said "Can you eat a project?" and hung up.
emotions: Stung and wronged, a little defiant (none of it said out loud).
meaning: He wants his father to recognise the path he chose; being hung up on left him no chance even to explain.
affect: a short, bitter laugh at the last line
flawed: It sounds like that didn't feel good.
error_note: "Didn't feel good" fits any event, so it names nothing. He was compared, dismissed and hung up on before he could finish — the feeling word needs to reach that.

background: Female, junior. Third session; the last two were about her relationship with her mother.
context:
Counsellor: Last time you said your mum tends to make decisions for you.
Client: Yeah. It happened again.
utterance: I wanted to spend the summer teaching at a rural school — I'd already been accepted. When my mum found out she said it's too hard, signed me up for an internship instead, and said "I'm doing this for you." And I know she is... I just don't want to go.
surface: She was accepted to a summer teaching programme; her mother, thinking it too hard, signed her up for an internship "for her"; she does not want to go.
emotions: Powerless and bypassed; guilty toward her mother ("I know she is").
meaning: What she cares about is making one choice of her own — the programme may matter less than wanting, for once, to go her own way and being overruled again.
affect: "I just don't want to go" said very quietly
flawed: Your mum's probably just worried about you. It really does come from a place of love.
error_note: This explains the third party: the conversation shifts from her feelings to her mother's motives. She has already said "I know she is" — she doesn't need that line; she needs someone to hear that she wanted to make this decision herself.

background: Male, senior. First session; the intake form says "want to talk before graduating".
context:
Counsellor: Where would you like to start?
Client: Well... I've been packing up my room.
utterance: While I was packing I found my first-year timetable. I'd written all these plans on it — join the debate team, learn guitar, go to Tibet. I didn't do any of them. And I graduate next month.
surface: Packing up, he found his first-year timetable with plans on it (debate team, guitar, Tibet); he did none of them; he graduates next month.
emotions: Wistful, some regret (unsaid).
meaning: He is measuring the person he meant to become in first year against who he is now; the regret is less about three activities than about four years not lived the way he wanted.
flawed: While you were packing you found your first-year timetable, none of the plans on it got done, and you graduate next month.
error_note: This restates the content accurately but stays on the surface. Reflecting meaning means catching the unspoken stake: he is measuring himself against his first-year self, and the regret is about four years not lived the way he'd hoped.

background: Female, second-year master's student. Second session; last time you talked about the internship and the thesis pulling in two directions.
context:
Counsellor: How has the week been?
Client: Messier.
utterance: My advisor says the internship is distracting me and my thesis is holding the whole lab back. But I found that internship myself — it's the only thing I actually find interesting. I don't know whose side to take.
surface: Her advisor says the internship distracts her and her thesis is slowing the lab; she found the internship herself and it is the only thing she finds interesting; she does not know whose side to take.
emotions: Anxious and squeezed, wronged, a little defiant.
meaning: She wants to protect the one thing she chose and cares about — a bit of herself she found in grad school; "whose side" hides whether she is allowed to speak up for what matters to her.
flawed: Maybe sit down with your advisor and show him a schedule for the internship and your thesis, so you can manage both.
error_note: This is advice: the plan may be workable, but what she said most forcefully was "the only thing I actually find interesting". Until that is caught, a plan just becomes one more task.

background: Female, junior, juggling a job and her studies. First session.
context:
Counsellor: Where would you like to start today?
Client: Just... I've been really busy.
utterance: I work at a bubble tea shop Monday to Friday evenings, and on weekends I tutor a middle schooler in maths. I had two midterms last week and I studied for them at the shop whenever it was quiet.
surface: Works weekday evenings at a bubble tea shop; tutors maths on weekends; had two midterms last week and studied at the shop during quiet moments
emotions: Tired; holding it together (unsaid).
meaning: She is keeping her life and her studies afloat on her own and wants that effort seen, not questioned with why she doesn't work less.
affect: talks fast, like reading out a schedule

background: Male, sophomore, clashing sleep schedules in his dorm. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Last time we talked about your room. How was this week?
Client: Same as before.
utterance: The guy in the top bunk games until two every morning and his keyboard is really loud. I asked him once, and he put headphones on, but the keyboard is still loud. I've got seven a.m. classes three days this week.
surface: Top-bunk roommate games until 2 a.m. every night; the keyboard is loud; he raised it once and the roommate put on headphones but the keyboard is still loud; three 7 a.m. classes this week
emotions: Irritated; worn out from lack of sleep.
meaning: He has already tried talking and it didn't fix it; he is unsure whether he can bring it up again without souring things.

background: Female, first-year master's student, recently moved far from home. First session.
context:
Counsellor: How long have you been here?
Client: A bit over two months.
utterance: There's no central heating here in winter, so I do my homework at night wrapped in a blanket. The food in the dining hall is all kind of sweet and I'm not used to it, so I mostly make instant noodles. My mum sends me a box of homemade smoked pork every week.
surface: No heating in winter, does homework wrapped in a blanket; dining hall food is too sweet for her, mostly eats instant noodles; her mum sends a box of homemade smoked pork every week
emotions: Homesick; not settling in (not said directly).
meaning: The small hardships all point to something unsaid: she hasn't found a sense of home here yet, and her mother's parcels are her link to it.

background: Male, first-year, injured during military training. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You said your foot still isn't better?
Client: Yeah, it's a torn ligament.
utterance: On the last day of military training I rolled my ankle and tore a ligament — six weeks to heal. I'm on crutches for class now, and it takes me twenty minutes to get from my dorm to the teaching building. I missed the basketball team tryouts too.
surface: Rolled his ankle on the last day of training, torn ligament, six weeks to heal; on crutches, twenty minutes from dorm to class; missed the basketball tryouts
emotions: Discouraged; disappointed.
meaning: He had hoped basketball would give him his place at university, and the injury has pushed that starting point back.

background: Female, senior, thesis stuck with her advisor. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: How's the thesis coming along?
Client: I'm stuck.
utterance: I've sent my advisor three drafts, and every time he just writes back "revise it a bit more" without saying what. I've gone to his office twice and missed him both times. The defence is in five weeks and the others in my group are already formatting.
surface: Sent three drafts; advisor only replies "revise it a bit more" without specifics; went to his office twice and missed him; defence in five weeks, groupmates already formatting
emotions: Anxious; at a loss; a little wronged.
meaning: She is willing to revise but gets no direction; what matters is putting in effort with nowhere to push it while watching herself fall behind.

background: Male, 28, quit his job after three years to study for an exam. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You said you made a decision recently?
Client: Yeah. I quit.
utterance: I quit my job last month to study for the civil service exam. My savings should last about a year. I haven't told my parents — they think I'm still working, so I wear a dress shirt every week when we video-call.
surface: Quit last month to prepare for the civil service exam; savings last about a year; hasn't told his parents; wears a dress shirt on weekly video calls to look like he's still working
emotions: Nervous; guilty toward his parents; the strain of hiding it.
meaning: He is giving himself a chance to start over but isn't ready to face his parents' reaction; hiding it buys the decision some time.

background: Female, sophomore, roommate hasn't repaid a loan. First session.
context:
Counsellor: What would you like to talk about first?
Client: Money. It sounds petty saying it.
utterance: My roommate borrowed two thousand from me last semester and said she'd pay it back when term started. Term's been going over a month now, she's bought a new phone, and she's telling us she's going to a concert this weekend. I brought it up once and she said "next month".
surface: Roommate borrowed 2,000 last semester, promised to repay when term started; over a month into term, not repaid; she bought a new phone and is going to a concert this weekend; raised it once and got "next month"
emotions: Resentful; not taken seriously; stuck.
meaning: It isn't only the money — it is whether she counts; she is also afraid that raising it again will damage a relationship she lives inside.

background: Male, second-year master's student, lopsided group project. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: How's the project going this week?
Client: It's pretty much just me.
utterance: There are four of us on the project, and I'm doing the data cleaning, the modelling and the report. The other three say they're preparing for internship interviews. It's due next Friday, and last night I was the only one who showed up to the meeting.
surface: Four-person project, he is doing the data cleaning, modelling and report; the other three say they're prepping for interviews; due next Friday; only he came to last night's meeting
emotions: Exhausted; sense of unfairness; carrying it alone.
meaning: He has quietly shouldered it, and what matters is that nobody shares the load or even notices it.

background: Female, 30, mother of two with a full-time job. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You said it was hard to find time to come?
Client: Yes, I took half a day off for this.
utterance: My older one's in primary school and someone has to pick her up at four every afternoon; the little one is eighteen months and still waking up at night. I work during the day, and by the time I've got both of them to sleep it's about eleven, and then I open my laptop to finish the work I didn't get to.
surface: Older child in primary school needs picking up at four; youngest is eighteen months and wakes at night; she works all day, gets both to sleep around eleven; then opens her laptop to finish work
emotions: Depleted; exhausted (said calmly).
meaning: She puts herself after everyone else, and almost none of her day belongs to her.

background: Male, junior, grandfather in hospital. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: How has this term been?
Client: Fine.
utterance: It's nothing really, I've just been going home a lot this term. My grandad's in hospital, so I go back every two weeks — five hours on the coach. When I'm back I catch up on classes with my friends' notes. It's fine, honestly, everyone's been really helpful.
surface: Grandfather in hospital, goes home every two weeks, five hours each way by coach; catches up with borrowed notes; says "it's fine" and "everyone's been really helpful"
emotions: Tired; worried (covered by "fine").
meaning: He is holding things together between two places; saying he's fine keeps others from worrying and keeps him from admitting how close he is to not coping.

background: Female, senior, three-year relationship just ended. First session.
context:
Counsellor: Your form just says "want to talk".
Client: Yeah, it's already sort of over, though.
utterance: We were together three years, and last week he said he didn't think it was working. It was calm, no fight. I boxed up his things and sent them back, and I logged out of his gaming account. It's just that I still check my phone out of habit when I wake up.
surface: Together three years, he ended it last week; calm, no fight; she mailed back his things and logged out of his gaming account; still checks her phone out of habit on waking
emotions: Loss; emptiness (unsaid).
meaning: She is holding the situation up with how calmly it was handled, but three years of habit remain and she hasn't let herself feel the loss.

background: Male, first-year master's student, loaded with errands by his advisor. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Has the research side started yet?
Client: Uh... still settling in.
utterance: This term I've filed four expense claims for my advisor, pulled together the close-out paperwork for two projects, and one weekend I helped him move house. Research? Hasn't started. But you learn things being around him, and I think that's pretty normal.
surface: Filed four expense claims, assembled close-out paperwork for two projects, helped his advisor move house one weekend; research hasn't started; says you learn from being around him and it's "pretty normal"
emotions: Resigned; quietly anxious (covered by "pretty normal").
meaning: He is finding reasons for his advisor's demands; underneath is worry that his research time is being eaten and he's falling behind.

background: Female, sophomore, younger brother sitting his university entrance exams. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: Did you go home over the break?
Client: Yeah, for a few days.
utterance: My brother's doing his entrance exams this year, so my mum turned the south-facing room into his study, and when I go home I sleep on the living-room sofa. Which makes sense, it's his final year. This time I stayed four days and then came back to campus — I said I had to prepare for a competition.
surface: Brother has entrance exams; mum made the south-facing room his study; she sleeps on the sofa when home; says "makes sense, it's his final year"; left after four days saying she had a competition to prepare for
emotions: Disappointed; overlooked (framed as "makes sense").
meaning: She justifies the arrangement, but leaving early gives away the feeling that there's no longer a place for her at home.

background: Male, 25, working in another city. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Anything on your mind this week?
Client: My best mate's getting married.
utterance: My best friend is getting married next month and asked me to be best man. The wedding's back home, and I checked — that week our project goes live, so I can't get leave. I sent him a cash gift and said I'd join by video. He said no worries, he understands.
surface: Best friend marrying next month, asked him to be best man; wedding is back home, project launches that week so no leave; sent a cash gift and promised a video call; friend said he understands
emotions: Regret; guilt (unsaid).
meaning: What he's missing isn't just a wedding but his closest friend's biggest moment; "he understands" makes it harder, not easier.

background: Female, first-year, first class presentation. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You said something from last week keeps coming back?
Client: Yeah. My presentation in class.
utterance: When it was my turn my hands wouldn't stop shaking, I skipped two slides by accident, and someone laughed out loud. When I finished I went back to my seat and kept my head down, and I didn't take in a single word for the rest of the class.
surface: Hands shaking during her presentation, skipped two slides; someone laughed out loud; went back to her seat head down; took in nothing for the rest of class
emotions: Embarrassed; ashamed; nervous.
meaning: She is afraid that one slip has fixed how everyone will see her from now on.

background: Male, junior, misjudged by his best friend. First session.
context:
Counsellor: What's been happening?
Client: My best mate won't talk to me.
utterance: My best mate thinks I told people his business, and now he won't answer my messages or reply to me in the group chat. I honestly never said anything. I sent him this long explanation and he just wrote back "ok".
surface: Best friend thinks he leaked his private business; not answering messages or replying in the group; he never said anything; long explanation got only "ok"
emotions: Wrongly accused; hurt; anxious.
meaning: He cares about the friendship, and being misread by the person he trusts most is the hardest part.

background: Female, second-year master's student, first paper accepted. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: You look different today.
Client: I've got good news!
utterance: My first paper got accepted yesterday! Three submissions and over a year of revisions. I actually shouted in the lab — I scared the guy at the next bench. The first thing I did was call my mum.
surface: First paper accepted; submitted three times, revised for over a year; shouted in the lab; called her mum first
emotions: Thrilled; proud; relieved.
meaning: More than a year of persistence has finally been recognised, and she wants to share it first with the person closest to her.

background: Male, sophomore, laptop stolen. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You said you really needed to talk today?
Client: I'm losing my mind.
utterance: My laptop got stolen in the library, and all my coursework project code from this term was on it — no backup. I reported it to the police, and campus security says the camera doesn't cover that corner. It's due next week.
surface: Laptop stolen in the library; the whole term's project code on it, no backup; reported to police, camera doesn't cover the spot; due next week
emotions: Panicked; kicking himself; helpless.
meaning: A whole term's work may be gone; he's blaming himself for not backing up and doesn't know how to recover.

background: Female, senior, roommates have all signed job offers. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: How's the week been?
Client: My room's going out to dinner tonight.
utterance: There are four of us in my room and three have signed offers. They're going out to celebrate tonight and they invited me, and I said sure. I'm genuinely happy for them — but when I picture sitting there and someone asking "what about you?", I want to find an excuse not to go.
surface: Three of four roommates have signed offers; they're celebrating tonight and invited her; she said yes; she's genuinely happy for them; dreads being asked "what about you?" and wants an excuse to skip
emotions: Happy for them yet stung; dreading the question; deflated.
meaning: It isn't that she can't be glad for her friends; the comparison makes her feel left behind and she is afraid of being seen that way.

background: Male, first-year master's student, parents' first visit to campus. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: How was your weekend?
Client: My parents came.
utterance: Last weekend my parents came to see me at uni for the first time — ten hours on the train. I showed them around, and my mum kept taking photos and telling anyone who'd listen "my son's doing his master's here". When I took them to the station that evening, my dad pressed an envelope into my hand with two thousand in it.
surface: Parents' first visit, ten hours by train; mum took photos and told people her son studies here; at the station his dad pressed an envelope with 2,000 into his hand
emotions: Moved; aching for them; guilty (all mixed).
meaning: He is touched by their pride and their sacrifice, and feels that at his age he is still the one taking from them.

background: Female, 25, new to work, team lead presented her proposal. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You wanted to talk about work?
Client: Yeah. Yesterday's meeting.
utterance: I spent two weeks, late nights, on that proposal. At the department meeting yesterday my team lead presented it without mentioning me once, and the director praised him on the spot for "really clear thinking". Afterwards he said to me, "Thanks for the hard work — I'll bring you along to present next time."
surface: Her two-week proposal presented by her team lead without mentioning her; director praised him for "really clear thinking"; afterwards he said thanks and he'd bring her next time
emotions: Angry; indignant; used.
meaning: She wants her work to be seen, and the casual "next time" makes the unfairness sharper.

background: Male, junior, his crush went public with a relationship. First session.
context:
Counsellor: What would you like to talk about?
Client: It's a bit embarrassing.
utterance: I've liked her for over a year and never said anything. Yesterday I saw a photo of her with a guy on social media, captioned "it's official". I liked the post. Then I went and ran ten laps of the track.
surface: Liked her over a year without telling her; saw her post announcing a relationship; liked the post; ran ten laps of the track
emotions: Deflated; heartbroken; regret at never saying it (none said).
meaning: He missed his chance and can only absorb it through a polite like and a run; the unsaid regret weighs the most.

background: Female, first-year master's student, pressured about marriage over the holidays. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: How was going home for New Year?
Client: Don't ask.
utterance: Over New Year my relatives took turns asking whether I was seeing anyone. In front of all of them my mum said "keep being this picky and no one will want you". I laughed and said I was busy with my studies, and then I went to my room and locked the door.
surface: Relatives took turns asking if she's seeing anyone; her mum said in front of everyone "keep being picky and no one will want you"; she laughed it off about studying; went to her room and locked the door
emotions: Humiliated; offended; hurt; angry (hidden behind a laugh).
meaning: What cuts deepest is that her mother publicly took the others' side; her own choices weren't respected.

background: Male, sophomore, missed out on a scholarship. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Anything new this week?
Client: The scholarship list came out.
utterance: The scholarship list came out and I'm not on it. Missed by one place. It's only a few thousand, it doesn't matter. I'm not studying for the money anyway. Funny thing is, the guy who got it copies my homework all the time.
surface: Missed the scholarship by one place; says it's only a few thousand and doesn't matter; not studying for money; the winner routinely copies his homework
emotions: Galled; indignant (pressed down by "doesn't matter").
meaning: What really bothers him is the unfairness: the one who did the work lost and the one who copied won.

background: Female, senior, father skipping her graduation. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: Graduation must be coming up?
Client: Yeah, next week.
utterance: My dad says he's got a work trip that day so he can't come. It's fine, my mum's coming. He'd only have taken a few photos anyway. He didn't come to my high school graduation either — I'm used to it.
surface: Father says a work trip means he can't come; mother will come; says he'd only have taken photos; he missed her high school graduation too — "I'm used to it"
emotions: Disappointed; hurt (called "used to it").
meaning: "Used to it" is protection built from being let down again and again; she has always hoped her father would show up for the moments that matter.

background: Male, third-year master's student, six months of data scrapped. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: How are the experiments going?
Client: Starting over. It's fine.
utterance: Six months of data, all thrown out because the instrument calibration was off. My advisor said redo it. I actually laughed and said "great, good practice". When I got back I put my lab notebook in a drawer and didn't go into the lab for two days.
surface: Calibration fault invalidated six months of data; advisor said redo it; he laughed and said "good practice"; put his notebook in a drawer and stayed out of the lab two days
emotions: Crushed; defeated; disheartened (masked by a joke).
meaning: The joke held the moment together, but two days away from the lab shows how hard it hit; he isn't sure he has it in him to start again.

background: Female, first-year, first birthday alone. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: It was your birthday a couple of days ago?
Client: Yeah, it was nice.
utterance: My birthday was the day before yesterday and my roommates had all gone home. I went downstairs and got myself a slice of cake, took a photo and posted it: "happy on my own too". Got loads of likes. It was nice.
surface: Birthday while roommates were away; bought herself a slice of cake and posted "happy on my own too"; got lots of likes; says "it was nice"
emotions: Lonely; let down (covered by "happy").
meaning: The happiness in the post was for other people; what she really felt was that nobody was with her that day.
affect: bright, then softer at the end

background: Male, 27, laid off. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You said you wanted to talk about a change at work?
Client: Yeah. I got let go.
utterance: The company did a round of layoffs and I was on the list. HR said it was restructuring, nothing personal, and the severance was by the book. I cleared my desk that same afternoon and said goodbye to everyone one by one. It was all very dignified.
surface: On the layoff list; HR said restructuring, not personal; severance by the book; cleared his desk that afternoon and said goodbye to each colleague; says it was "very dignified"
emotions: Shocked; deflated; feeling unneeded (held up by "dignified").
meaning: He is working hard to keep his dignity; underneath is the blow of being suddenly dismissed and doubt about his own worth.

background: Female, junior, summer volunteer teaching in a mountain village. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: How was your summer?
Client: I went volunteer teaching, for a month.
utterance: I spent a month over the summer teaching at a school in the mountains. On the day I left, a little girl pressed a drawing into my hand — it was me standing at the front of the class. She said "Miss, when I grow up I'm going to be a teacher too." I cried the whole bus ride.
surface: A month teaching in a mountain school; a girl gave her a drawing of her at the front of the class; the girl said she'd become a teacher too; she cried the whole bus ride
emotions: Moved; sad to leave.
meaning: She discovered that her being there truly shaped a child; feeling needed and worthwhile matters deeply to her and has her thinking about who she wants to become.

background: Male, sophomore, grandfather's old watch. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: That's an unusual watch.
Client: It was my grandad's.
utterance: My grandad died last year and left me an old watch that stopped working ages ago. I took it to be repaired and the man said parts are hard to find — fixing it would cost more than a new one. I had him fix it anyway.
surface: Grandfather died last year and left an old watch that no longer runs; repairer said fixing it costs more than a new one; he had it fixed anyway
emotions: Missing him; cherishing it.
meaning: Fixing the watch keeps his connection to his grandfather alive; its worth has nothing to do with price.

background: Female, first-year master's student, six months of morning runs. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Anything lately that made you happy?
Client: Yes! The fitness test.
utterance: For six months I've got up at six every morning and run five kilometres — not missed a single day. At the fitness test last week I ran the 800 metres in under four minutes. In high school I never even passed it.
surface: Ran 5 km every morning at six for six months without missing a day; ran the 800 m in under four minutes last week; never passed it in high school
emotions: Proud; excited.
meaning: She has proved to herself that she can change; getting from never passing to this has given her back her belief in herself.

background: Male, senior, learned to cook over the winter break. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: What did you get up to at home over the break?
Client: I learned to cook.
utterance: Over the break I learned to make braised pork belly from videos online. My mum had one bite and said "that's better than mine". My dad didn't say anything, but he went back for seconds twice.
surface: Learned braised pork belly from videos; mum said it was better than hers; dad said nothing but went back for more rice twice
emotions: Happy; satisfied.
meaning: Cooking is his way of looking after his parents, and his father's silent second helpings are exactly the recognition he wanted.

background: Female, sophomore, gave up an exchange programme. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: Last time you mentioned the exchange application?
Client: I didn't send it.
utterance: I'd planned to go on exchange in third year and had all the application materials ready. Last month my dad's business took a hit, so I didn't submit. I told my parents I'd just decided I didn't want to go, and they didn't ask.
surface: Planned an exchange in third year with materials ready; didn't submit after her father's business took a hit; told her parents she didn't want to go; they didn't ask
emotions: Regret; aching for her parents; a little hurt.
meaning: She chose to carry some of the family's weight and presented the sacrifice as her own wish so her parents wouldn't feel guilty; but no one knows what she gave up.

background: Male, second-year master's student, sticking with an unfashionable research area. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Have you settled on your research direction?
Client: My advisor's telling me to switch again.
utterance: All the senior students in my group have moved to large language models — you publish faster. I'm still annotating dialect speech data, and my advisor keeps telling me to switch. But every time I'm transcribing dialect recordings, I think of how my grandmother talked.
surface: Senior labmates moved to large models, which publish faster; he still annotates dialect data and his advisor urges him to switch; transcribing dialect recordings reminds him of his grandmother's voice
emotions: Torn; pressured; a quiet resolve.
meaning: What he's holding onto isn't just a topic but his tie to his grandmother and the language of home — something "publishes faster" can't measure.

background: Female, 28, bank employee thinking of opening a pottery studio. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You said something's been on your mind?
Client: Yes, though it sounds unrealistic saying it.
utterance: I've been at the bank five years, the pay's good, and my parents are thrilled. On weekends I help out at a pottery studio, and the owner says I've got really steady hands. Lately I've been working out what it would cost to open a small studio of my own. I've run the numbers three times.
surface: Five years at a bank, good pay, parents very pleased; helps at a pottery studio on weekends, owner says she has steady hands; has costed a small studio three times
emotions: Drawn to it; hesitant; uneasy.
meaning: She is standing between security and what she loves; running the numbers again and again is testing whether she dares take a risk for the life she wants.

background: Male, first-year, ran out of money early. First session.
context:
Counsellor: You said things have been a bit hard?
Client: It's about money.
utterance: I've still got a week left this month and my allowance is almost gone. My mum works the till at a supermarket — she makes a bit over three thousand a month. I'm too embarrassed to ask for more, so this week I'm just going to eat steamed buns.
surface: Allowance almost gone with a week left; his mother is a supermarket cashier earning a little over 3,000 a month; too embarrassed to ask for more; plans to eat only steamed buns this week
emotions: Guilty; embarrassed.
meaning: He refuses to become a burden on his mother and protects both his care for her and his own pride by going without.

background: Female, third-year master's student, packing up the room she's lived in for seven years. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Busy with graduation?
Client: Packing up my room.
utterance: I've lived in this room for seven years — undergrad plus my master's. While I was packing I found the letters the four of us wrote to ourselves ten years from now back in first year. We promised to open them together at graduation. Now I'm the only one still at this university.
surface: Seven years in the same dorm room; found letters the four roommates wrote to their future selves in first year, promised to open them at graduation; she's the only one still at the university
emotions: Nostalgic; wistful; lonely.
meaning: The letters hold a stretch of growing up together; being the only one left makes her feel those friendships and that youth slipping away.

background: Male, junior, didn't run for student union president. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: The student union elections must be over?
Client: Yeah. I didn't run.
utterance: Everyone assumed I'd run for president — I've been in the department two years. On registration day I didn't sign up, and I told them I wanted more time to study. It's nothing really, being president is just a lot of hassle. Besides, if I got elected and did a bad job, what would people think?
surface: Two years in the department, everyone expected him to run; didn't register; told others he wanted more study time; says being president is just hassle; worries what people would think if he did badly
emotions: Hesitant; uneasy; afraid of letting people down (covered by "nothing really").
meaning: He cares a great deal about others' expectations and judgement; stepping back isn't lack of interest but fear of falling short, a way of protecting himself from being seen to fail.

background: Female, senior, mother still displays her childhood drawing. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: You mentioned your mum last time?
Client: Yeah. Some of what she does is hard to figure out.
utterance: My mum framed a drawing I did as a kid and it's been hanging in the living room for more than ten years. I told her it's ugly and to take it down and she won't. Honestly it's a really bad drawing. I don't know why she keeps it.
surface: Childhood drawing framed in the living room for over ten years; she asked her mother to take it down and she refused; says it's a bad drawing; doesn't know why her mother keeps it
emotions: Embarrassed; quietly touched (while dismissing it).
meaning: She waves it away, but she is moved that her mother has treasured her all along; the drawing stands for being valued unconditionally.
affect: a smile at the corner of her mouth

background: Male, first-year master's student, turned down a big-tech internship. Second session.
context:
Counsellor: Have you sorted out an internship?
Client: Yeah, a small company.
utterance: My advisor recommended me for an internship at a big tech company — people fight over those. I turned it down and chose a small company that does hearing-aid algorithms. My classmates think I'm an idiot. Maybe I am. My cousin's worn hearing aids since he was little.
surface: Turned down a big-tech internship his advisor recommended; chose a small company building hearing-aid algorithms; classmates call him an idiot; his cousin has worn hearing aids since childhood
emotions: Settled yet unsettled by being doubted (jokes "maybe I am").
meaning: His choice is tied to his cousin — he wants to do work that truly helps people close to him; "idiot" is other people's yardstick, and what he cares about is the meaning of the work.

background: Female, 26, getting married next month. First session.
context:
Counsellor: Busy with the wedding?
Client: Yes, it's basically all sorted.
utterance: The wedding's next month and everything's booked. Yesterday while I was sorting through my things I found the hair ties my dad used to do my plaits with, and I actually put them in the box that's going to the new flat. It's a bit silly — I'm a grown woman.
surface: Wedding next month, everything booked; found the hair ties her father used for her plaits; packed them in the box for the new flat; says it's silly at her age
emotions: Reluctant to let go; nostalgic (brushed off as "silly").
meaning: Before leaving the home she grew up in, she wants to carry the childhood of being cared for by her father with her; getting married is also a goodbye.

background: Male, sophomore, left his band. Third session.
context:
Counsellor: How's the band these days?
Client: I quit.
utterance: I quit the band — didn't really think twice. Back in high school we said we'd play together for life, and now they're all busy with grad school applications and internships. Last rehearsal I was the only one who turned up. I sat in the practice room all afternoon, packed up the drums and left.
surface: Quit the band, says he didn't think twice; in high school they vowed to play together for life; others busy with applications and internships; he alone came to the last rehearsal, sat all afternoon, packed the drums and left
emotions: Deflated; lonely; left behind ("didn't think twice").
meaning: He was left before he left; the promise of "for life" had already come apart, and quitting marks the end of something that was already over.
